sect1.title: Setting up postfix
sect1.para: To remind ourself where we are in the overall setup process the setup of postfix will make it possible to send mails from our own machine by connecting to a running postfix daemon via the SMTP(S) protocol.

All relevant postfix configuration files can be found in the /etc/postfix/ directory. In the first instance we will setup postfix using a regular SMTP connection without the added complexity of a SSL/TLS certificate. Once we have this working we will modify the configuration to use the same key and certificate we created for Dovecot. This will work just fine as long as Dovecot and the SMTP server are running on the same host. If they are running on separate hosts a separate and unique certificate for postfix must be created since each server with unique IP address must have its own certificate (to avoid warnings from clients connecting to them).
In postfix there are two files in the /etc/postfix directory. we need to update:

listitem.para: main.cf - This is where all settings are stored, one huge parameter file
master.cf - This file controls what helper processes are started and on what ports they are listening.

caution.para: The changes you make manually in the postfix configuration might come into conflict if you later on decide to use Yast setup for the mail server. So don’t use the YAST setup once you have manually configured postfix (into perfection!). Actually we would recommend against using Yast mail server setup for any serious mail server since the tuning possibilities are near to zero.

Also, please be careful when editing the configuration file and watch out for setting the correct server variable. Sender or receiver, i.e. with prefix smtp_<variable> or smtpd_<variable> this is a common source of errors that can be surprisingly time consuming to find.

sect2.title: User authentication in postfix
sect2.para: Before we continue we need to discuss how postfix handles user authentication. When do we need that? By default postfix restricts who can use our server to send mail based on IP address. It will allow clients on the same sub-network as the server. However, with mobile usage we will most likely connect to our postfix server through a broadband router and then the router will forward our request to the server. Hence the request looks like it is coming from our sub-network (our gateway) and will be allowed. This would then allow anyone that knows our official IP address to the gateway (and the port to use) to use our SMTP server to send mail that looks like it is coming from us! This is what is known as an open relay and is something really bad.

So, we need a way to authenticate users before they are allowed to send mail via the SMTP server. By itself postfix has no built-in method for this. Instead it is constructed to use an external library which implements an API known as SASL (Simple Authentications and Security Layer). The SASL library is a completely independent of postfix. There are several available providers of a compliant SASL library (for example the SASL authentication daemon saslauthd). The good news here is that Dovecot provides one possible implementation of a SASL library. Since we already have Dovecot installed it seems a good idea to use it. As you may recall we made some provisions for this when we configured Dovecot (even though we didn't explain the details at the time).
So after we have configured postfix to use the Dovecot SASL the following happens when a user connects.

listitem.para: Postfix send the authentication details through the SASL API to Dovecot

Dovecot receives the authentication details and uses the configured way to lookup the user details. By default dovecot uses the Linux PAM framework which normally is configured to check the user and password from the shadow password file. This requires all mail users to also have an account on the server. Dovecot can also use other methods such as an LDAP server or even a database with all the user credentials stored. The main advantage with storing users in a DB is that they do not need to have user accounts on the server.
Dovecot returns fail or success to postfix which based on this knows whether to accept or reject the incoming call.

sect2.para: There is still one problem with this authentication setup in that the user and passwords are sent in plain text over the network. For automatic network sniffers this is a gold mine since harvesting valid user/passwords combos is what spammers are after. The way to protect our conversation is to use SSL/TLS encryption of the communication between the client and the server in the same way we protected the IMAP and https:// traffic.

note.para: SSL (Secure Socket Layer) was renamed TLS (Transport Layer Security) by the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) as of version 3.1. There are some technical differences between SSL and TLS but for all practical reasons (as far as we are concerned) they are the same.

sect3.title: Configuring Dovecot SASL in postfix
sect3.para: Assuming we keep the network settings as default (allowing clients from the same sub-network to connect). We need to add/change the following settings in the postfix configuration file.
sect3.programlisting: smtpd_sasl_auth_enable = yes broken_sasl_auth_clients = yes smtpd_sasl_type = dovecot smtpd_sasl_path = private/auth smtpd_sasl_security_options = noanonymous
sect3.para: Then add permit_sasl_authenticated to the smtpd_recipient_restrictions section as the following example shows
The order of these restrictions are important as it is to finish with reject_unauth_destination since by default the connection will just “fall through” and be allowed !

sect3.title: Configuring postfix to use our ISPs SMTP server
sect3.para: If your server, like most home servers, does not have a fixed IP address you cannot send mails directly from your home server since all official mail servers on the internet must have a fixed IP address and have a so called, MX record in the DNS server which identifies the server as a Mail eXchange server. Hence we must go through another proper mail server to send mail. This other mail server is usually our ISPs server (but it doesn’t have to be). This is known as making our SMTP server a relay server (since it relays mail to this other proper mail server).

Most likely we also need to give a username/password in order for us to be able to login to our ISPs mail server. In the following we assume that our ISP:s mail server is called “smtp.ourisp.com” and accepts connection not on the standard port 25 but on port 26 (just to show how to handle other ports)

sect3.title: Verifying postfix SASL connection
sect3.para: Before moving on we should make sure that this works as we have intended. We can do this in the same way as we tested the IMAP connection, by hand. This allows us to see the core protocol level without any client getting in our way.

When you configure your mail clients later, they will handle this authentication process automatically - you won't need to manually encode passwords. The client will prompt you for your username and password, then use the SASL mechanism we've configured here to authenticate securely. If authentication fails when you set up your client, first verify that you can login successfully using these manual tests, then check that your client is configured to use the correct authentication method (typically "Normal password" or "PLAIN" in client settings).

Escape character is '^]'. 220 myserver.com ESMTP Postfix EHLO myserver.com 250-myserver.com 250-PIPELINING 250-SIZE 250-VRFY 250-ETRN 250-AUTH PLAIN 250-AUTH=PLAIN 250-ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES 250-8BITMIME 250 DSN AUTH PLAIN AHVzZXIAdXNlcnBhc3N3ZA== 235 2.7.0 Authentication successful quit 221 2.0.0 Bye Connection closed by foreign host.

sect3.para: We also want to have any system mail for root delivered to a “real” user. For this we need to setup an alias for root. This is done by making sure that the file /etc/aliases has a line

where <user> is a real existing user that will receive the root mails. After you have updated this file you need to run the command “newaliases” which will produce the file alias.db based on the original alias file.

sect3.title: Rewriting sender addresses
sect3.para: If a mail is sent from the local user on a server that is not directly connected to the internet it will have a domain name that in most cases are “fake”, for example joe@localhost.nil (this will of course depend on what name you have given the server). The problem with this is twofold. First the recipient cannot answer to this address and secondly most mail servers requires that the from-address is a valid (can be looked up in DNS) to forward the mail at all.

To correct this situation postfix has the ability to rewrite your “bad” addresses to something the recipient can actually answer to. In fact, a lot of the complexity in postfix comes from the various ways of rewriting addresses. Here we will just use the most basic rewrite functionality. For a fuller (and very readable) discussion on the rewrite options in postfix consult the postfix HowTo “Postfix Address Rewriting” available on the postfix website.
This type of address rewriting is also known as address “masquerading” (for obvious reasons).

In order to have postfix translate the “bad” mail address to a “good” address a file with mappings between “bad” and “good” must be created. In this case we will use a map/file called “sender_canonical”. For example, assuming that “joe” want all his sent mail to look like it is coming from his GMail account joe@gmail.com we then add the following line to the sender_canonical file

sect3.title: Installing certificates
sect3.para: As mentioned above we can use the same certificates we created for dovecot as long as postfix is running on the same server as Dovecot (same IP address).
The certificate and key we created for Dovecot were shown in . We must now tell postfix to enable SSL/TLS for incoming connections as well as point postfix to those certificates that we want to use.
To do this we update main.cf as shown below
sect3.programlisting: smtpd_tls_security_level = may smtpd_tls_key_file = /etc/ssl/private/dovecot.pem smtpd_tls_cert_file = /etc/ssl/certs/dovecot.pem smtpd_tls_loglevel = 1 tls_random_source = dev:/dev/urandom smtpd_tls_auth_only = yes

note.para: and tells postfix to use TLS.
For debugging purposes the loglevel can be increased to ‘2’.

The final setting, smtpd_tls_auth_only = yes, forces the use of TLS for SASL authentication and will not allow plain text authentication to occur unless a SSL/TLS session has been established. (It may therefore be useful to comment out smtpd_tls_auth_only = yes during testing.)

sect3.title: Accessing an encrypted server
sect3.para: Historically a separate port have been used for the encrypted version of the SMTP protocol when SSL was used. With SSL (and not TLS!) this is needed since the entire conversation is encrypted so the server listening on the port has to use encryption from the start. The only real user noticeable difference between SSL and TLS is that with the modern TLS it is possible to start the conversation non-encrypted and as soon as both client and server has agreed to use encryption the rest of the conversation is encrypted. One of the big advantages with TLS is therefore that it is possible to use the same port for both encrypted and non-encrypted traffic (as defined by RFC 3207) .
This means that we now have a choice on how we setup the actual access to the server over the encrypted connections.

listitem.para: Use a dedicated port (old way) with SSL or
Use the same port with TLS

sect3.para: For all modern installation it is strongly recommended to use the modern way with the same port using TLS.

sect3.title: Using a dedicated port for encrypted traffic
sect3.para: Again, this is NOT the recommended way but is included for completion. Unless you know that some clients only support this way you should not implement this.

Originally port 465 was used as the separate SSL port for encrypted SMTP or SMTPS (sometimes also referred to as SSMTP). Unfortunately this port assignment was never made official as far as IANA recognized port numbers go. Instead it is registered for URD – “URL Rendesvous Directory for SSM” by Cisco.

In addition the original intention of port 465 was to let SMTP servers forward mail between each other over an encrypted channel. It was never intended to be used by mail clients to talk to the server directly. For this purpose another port was to be used, port 587 “Message submission” (see RFC 2476).

So using this older setup an SMTP server was really supposed to be listening on three ports. Port 25 for normal unencrypted traffic both from other servers and from clients, port 465 to allow other servers to communicate and finally port 587 to allow mail clients to submit new mails.

However, reality doesn't necessarily always match the theory. Most servers only use two port, one for unencrypted and one for encrypted traffic. Even though technically incorrect most servers use port 465 for SMTPS (both from clients and other severs).

For a home based server (which does not have a DNS entry as a registered MX server connected directly to the internet as an official mail server) it doesn't really matter if you choose the common (but incorrect) port 465 or port 587 as long as you configure your clients correctly on which port they should use to send mails. The only thing you need to watch out for when using port 465 is that since this is not an officially assigned port for SMTPS one extra step is needed as described below.

para.emphasis: Using port 465 for encrypted SMTP traffic

sect3.para: Since port 465 is not an officially recognized port for SMTPS we must either update /etc/services (that is a file which lists all officially recognized ports and gives symbolic names to them) to be able to use the symbolic name “smtps” for the port in our master.cnf postfix or use the port number directly.
To use the symbolic name we must add the line
to /etc/services and remove any other service registered to that port. The entry in /etc/services is only made to be able to refer to the port number with a symbolic name.

The next step is to instruct postfix to listen on this port and enable the manger process that handles the TLS connections for postfix. This is done by editing master.cf and first removing the comment for the following line:

para.programlisting: smtps inet n - n - - SMTPD –o smtpd_tls_wrappermode=yes

sect3.para: and then removing the comment for the line
For these new settings to take place we now need to restart postfix

tip.para: As alternative you could skip the editing of /etc/services and just enter the numeric port number directly in master.cnf but this is a more “hackery” way of administer a server. It’s best to have all the services recognized on the server listed in /etc/services.

para.emphasis: Using port 587 for encrypted SMTP traffic

sect3.para: Since port 587 is an officially recognized port there is no need to update /etc/services . The only update needed is to remove the comments in master.cnf for the two lines
and
This will enable the server to listen on port 587.

If you look in the master.cnf file you will also see that by default some optional parameters are give directly on the command line. The parameters are mirrors of the ones given in the main.cnf but will take precedence. The command line parameters are useful when you need different set of parameters for different ports.

Actually port 587 should really be used for submitting emails even if no encryption is used. Unfortunately many commercial providers do not follow this recognized standard and just assumes that both clients and other servers would contact them on port 25.
If you want to use port 587 for submission with only optional encryption for those client requesting this just remove the “smtpd_tls_auth_only = yes” option and SSL/TLS encryption will be optional.

sect3.title: Using the same port for both encrypted and non-encrypted traffic
sect3.para: This is the recommended way for a modern secure SMTP server setup.

With this method no extra ports are needed. Instead the normal port 25 is used for both encrypted and non encrypted traffic. When a client first connects to the server it will notice the by the servers response that TLS is supported (by the STARTTLS response code) and if the client is also capable of TLS encryption it might then ask the server to continue the rest of the conversation using SSL/TLS encryption.
To enable this method it suffices to enable the tlsmgr by uncommenting the line
in master.cnf

This might seem contradictory to what we recommended in the previous paragraph regarding the use of port 587. Technically you would be correct. The advantage is that some poorly written clients will only support port 25. In addition keeping as few ports open as possible is a good thing from a security point.

This is simply case where there simply is no single one correct answer. The official standard stipulates one thing but years of de-facto standard shows something else. Most (all?) ISP do not even allow incoming traffic on port 587 (which they really should!) and many clients only support port 25 for unencrypted submission and port 465 for encrypted submission (which technically is the wrong way of doing it).

sect3.title: Verifying the SSL/TLS setup when using a different SSL port
sect3.para: Finally we need to verify our setup. To verify that SSL/TLS is enabled in postfix we start by open a plain telnet session to postfix on the normal (non-secure) port 25

para.screen: $> telnet localhost 25 telnet localhost 25 Trying ::1... Connected to localhost. Escape character is '^]'. 220 myserver.com ESMTP Postfix EHLO myserver.com 250-myserver.com 250-PIPELINING 250-SIZE 250-VRFY 250-ETRN 250-STARTTLS 250-ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES 250-8BITMIME 250 DSN quit 221 2.0.0 Bye Connection closed by foreign host.

sect3.para: The thing to notice above is the absence of AUTH PLAIN (since we disabled that unless we had a secure connection which we don’t have since we connected with telnet) and the addition of 250-STARTTLS which indicates that postfix is ready to accept a secure connection over TLS
The rest of the section assumes that the server has been setup to listen on port 465 for secure connections.
The next step therefore is to verify the encrypted connection in the same way as we did for the IMAP server using the “openssl s_client” command (see s_client(1) for more details).
This will first give you a long list of SSL/TLS details and in the end you will see a line like

You can then give the EHLO myserver.com command to see what capabilities are supported and it should be the same as in the previous telnet session but without the STARTTLS info line since we are already in a TLS session but with the AUTH PLAIN (and AUTH=PLAIN) indicating that postfix is ready to accept an incoming login. After this you should also try to login in the same way we did without SSL/TLS (just remember the base64 encoding).
Once this is working you should try to access the SMTP server using the full IP address or hostname, for example as

Either remove the line completely or add the IP address of the host to the line, i.e. in this case.
